paras: The attempted lynching of Jim Offutt took place at about 1 a.m. on a Friday in late July 1881, when a large body of masked men came to the jail in Paris, Bourbon County, Kentucky, and demanded Offutt, a prisoner accused of frightening a woman to death. The jailer escaped with the keys and raised an alarm, and the men withdrew when townspeople filled the streets. A Georgia paper cited the episode as one town's stand against lynch law, and Offutt was shot dead by his brother-in-law about three weeks later.

According to a Paris dispatch printed after his death, Offutt and William H. Current, brothers-in-law, had quarreled some weeks earlier, and Offutt then wanted Current's life. Offutt was said to have gone to Current's house with a shotgun while Current was away and threatened to kill him on sight, and Mrs. Current was thrown into spasms and died. The longer version of the dispatch attributed her death to the spasms together with "sickness attendant upon premature childbirth."

Offutt was arrested "after some difficulty" and lodged in the jail at Paris. The Stanford Interior Journal described him as "a notorious murderer and bully," and the dispatch called him perhaps "the most noted and desperate man in the Blue Grass region."

At 1 o'clock on a Friday morning, "a large body of masked men" appeared at the jail and demanded the prisoner. The jailer had already left with the keys, and in the Interior Journal's account he rang the town bell "so loudly and persistently" that large numbers of people came into the street. Faced with the crowd, the lynchers retired without the prisoner, and no one was reported hurt.

No arrest of any member of the mob was reported, and the masked men were never named. Offutt was later admitted to bail in the sum of $2,000, which he secured. On Aug. 22 or 23 he met Current in the road near Ewalt's Cross Roads, and Current shot and killed him; the Interior Journal said Offutt drew his pistol first. No report of an inquest or of any charge against Current appears in the coverage.

The attempt itself drew only brief notice, all in white papers, and none stated the race of Offutt or of the mob. The Memphis Daily Appeal ran it as a two-sentence regional item on Aug. 5, the same day the Interior Journal printed its fuller paragraph. Outside Kentucky the story became material for comment: the Martinsburg Independent said the mob was "frightened off by the ringing of the fire bells" and jibed that Kentucky was still called the land of "brave men," while the Marietta Journal wrote that the people of "one Kentucky town, at least, do not approve of lynch law."

Offutt's death reached a wider audience through a Paris wire dispatch carried in New York, Chicago, Memphis, Yankton and Cheyenne under headings such as "A Desperado Killed" and "A Tragic Affair in Kentucky," none of which mentioned the earlier mob. The short version called the killing "Corrert's retribution," with Current's name misprinted. The Interior Journal recalled the foiled lynching in its notice of the death and said that "the people rejoice that his end has come," adding that the law hardly ever punished such men but justice overtook them in a way "far more effective." The Hopkinsville South Kentuckian reported the killing in a single line of state news.

Accounts differ on the alarm: the Interior Journal said the jailer rang the town bell, the Martinsburg paper spoke of fire bells, and the Marietta paper of church bells. Versions of the later dispatch also give Offutt's middle initial as S. or T. and place his killing on Monday or Tuesday.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A body of masked men came to the Paris jail at night to take and lynch a prisoner, Jim Offutt, and withdrew without him when the jailer fled with the keys and the town turned out (A1, A2, A4).

The mob sought to lynch Offutt for causing a woman's death, an extralegal act under the pretext of justice, but it was driven off and he was not harmed (A1, A2, A10); he was killed weeks later by one man, his brother-in-law, not by a group (A6, A10).

Two reports printed the same day in Memphis and Stanford, Ky., with different details (the jailer's escape with the keys in both, the bell only in the Kentucky paper), agree on the foiled attempt, and a later Kentucky account confirms it (A1, A2, A10).

accounts.label: Kentucky news items
accounts.gist: Masked men came into Paris at night to lynch the jailed Offutt; the jailer escaped with the keys and rang the town bell, and the crowd that gathered caused the lynchers to retire.

accounts.label: Out-of-state comment
accounts.gist: A West Virginia paper said the mob was frightened off by fire bells; a Georgia paper said church bells were rung and residents chased the lynchers away.

accounts.label: Interior Journal retrospective
accounts.gist: After Offutt's killing, the Stanford paper recounted the threats, the arrest and the mob 'frightened off by the prompt action of the jailer', and welcomed his death.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal ran the attempt as a two-sentence regional item ending 'the mob foiled'.

The Interior Journal named Offutt 'a notorious murderer and bully' and later 'one of the worst men that ever lived in that section', saying 'the people rejoice' at his death and that justice overtakes such men when the law does not, while reporting the lynchers' retreat without comment.
The Martinsburg Independent used the retreat to mock Kentucky's reputation for 'brave men', without comment on lynching itself.
The Marietta Journal said the people of 'one Kentucky town, at least, do not approve of lynch law'.
